news.title: Bangladesh hands death sentences to 7 aides of ousted Prime Minister Hasina
news.raw_text:
Bangladesh hands death sentences to 7 aides of ousted Prime Minister Hasina
Seven members of ousted PM Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League convicted of crimes including murder, provoking killings.
Seven aides of ousted Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina have been sentenced to death in absentia on charges relating to their roles in trying to crush the country’s 2024 uprising.
The seven men, members of ousted leader Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League, were convicted of crimes against humanity, including murder, as well as instigating and provoking killings.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Bangladesh protesters demand action over rising costs
- list 2 of 3Why Bangladesh has lost 1,000 lives to measles despite record vaccine drive
- list 3 of 3Bangladesh holds presidential election in first contested vote in 35 years
A three-member tribunal in Dhaka, headed by Justice Nazrul Islam Chowdhury, issued the sentences on Tuesday.
Those convicted include former state minister for information and broadcasting, Mohammad Ali Arafat, and Hasina’s Awami League party General-Secretary Obaidul Quader, who were charged with murder as well as instigating killings.
Sixty-eight people have been convicted in cases related to the crackdown, and 22 have been given death sentences. Only four are currently in custody.
Hasina, 78, was sentenced to death by hanging last November for charges of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown on the 2024 uprising that led to her fleeing the country she had ruled for 15 years.
State-appointed defence lawyer M Hasan Imam said the seven men were not directly involved in the killings and that the court could have handed down a lesser sentence than death.
“They were not directly involved in the killings; they have been convicted due to their fellow activists and supporters,” he said.
The other five men are AFM Bahauddin Nasim, Sheikh Fazle Shams Parash, Mainul Hossain Khan Nikhil, Saddam Hussain and Sheikh Wali Asif Enan.
The tribunal also ordered the confiscation of half the assets belonging to the five men, saying that they will be distributed as compensation to the families of those who died or were injured during the crackdown.
During the uprising, up to 1,400 people were killed, and thousands were injured by Hasina’s security forces and her supporters, according to the United Nations.
Since fleeing the country, Hasina has been living in exile in India, but she said she will return to Bangladesh by the end of the year, in December.
news.summary: Hasina, 78, was sentenced to death by hanging last November for charges of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown on the 2024 uprising that led to her fleeing the country she had ruled for 15 years. “They were not directly involved in the killings; they have been convicted due to their fellow activists and supporters,” he said.

news.title: FBI Director Kash Patel testifies before Senate panel as Democrats blast his record, FBI touts crime stats
news.raw_text:
FBI Director Kash Patel testifies before Senate panel as Democrats blast his record, FBI touts crime stats
What to know about Kash Patel's testimony:
- FBI Director Kash Patel is appearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday for an annual hearing on oversight of the FBI.
- Patel touted the murder rate falling to a 20-year low, saying it was "no easy effort," and he said all 10 people on the FBI's most wanted list had been apprehended during his tenure.
- Patel has been under scrutiny over a raft of firings and resignations from the bureau and for some of his behavior, including his use of the FBI jet. In May, the FBI director also clashed with Democratic senators over allegations of excessive drinking.
Durbin pushes Patel on the FBI not investigating shootings involving law enforcement
Sen. Durbin pushed Patel on whether the FBI has properly investigated the federal officer-involved shootings in Illinois, accusing the bureau of not investigating multiple shootings during the Trump administration's federal law enforcement surge in the state last year.
"Director Patel, why has the FBI refused to investigate either of these shootings?" Durbin said, referring to the shooting of Marimar Martinez by a border patrol agent and the killing of Silverio Villegas Gonzalez by an ICE agent last year.
Patel defended the bureau, saying there are investigations that are "ongoing" and he could not comment on them.
"We are not the only agency involved, since it involves multiple federal agencies," Patel said. "So we have to work with our federal and state and local partners to collect the information and allow the Department of Justice to make whatever decision they deem appropriate."
Patel says the 10th individual on the FBI's most wanted list has been apprehended: "That's 10 out of 10"
Patel announced the FBI captured an individual he described as "a thug down in Venezuela who was on our most wanted list and on the run for years."
"He has been captured, apprehended and is on his way back to the United States of America," Patel added. Patel said the individual represented the tenth individual on the list of the FBI's most wanted individuals.
"That's 10 of 10," Patel said. "Nobody in the FBI's history has done that."
Patel says "this FBI's made America safer than it's ever been"
In his opening statement, Patel touted the FBI's work under his leadership, calling it "the most prolific run of crime reduction in United States history." He pointed to figures on the arrests of violent criminals and gang members and the removal of more than 3,000 kilograms of fentanyl, among other statistics.
"This FBI is making America safe," Patel said.
Patel also touted the U.S. murder rate falling to a 20-year low, calling it "no easy effort." And he said "the success means that this FBI's made America safer than it's ever been."
Patel cited changes at the FBI, including adding task force officers and building a strategic information center to modernize the Bureau. And he nodded to his confirmation hearing in 2025, saying at the time, he told the committee "that the FBI needed to be faster, more efficient, eliminate bureaucracy and reduce the weaponization of law enforcement completely, embrace technological advancements, and engage with our partners, and most importantly, let good cops be cops."
"Under President Trump's leadership, I'm proud to say we've not only accelerated that mission, we have delivered," he said.
Durbin criticizes Patel in opening statement for his work on Trump-ordered investigations into his political opponents, 2020 election
Sen. Dick Durbin, the ranking member on the Senate Judiciary Committee, criticized Patel's credentials in his opening statement, calling him the "least qualified and most partisan FBI director in our nation's history."
The Illinois Democrat criticized Patel's involvement in the ongoing Justice Department "grand conspiracy" investigation, investigation into Obama and Biden-era officials who President Trump has accused, so far without evidence, of attempting to keep him out of political office.
"Director Patel has been the central figure pushing the so-called 'grand conspiracy,' diverting FBI resources to inane, debunked conspiracy theories that the quote deep state has been targeting President Trump since his first campaign," Durbin said. Durbin also criticized Patel for continuing to investigate 2020 the election results in states like Georgia, where former President Biden beat Mr. Trump to secure the presidency.
Durbin also said that Patel has "gutted" hiring standards, citing CBS News' recent reporting that the standards have been relaxed for FBI applicants who had stolen from previous employers, or engaged in sex solicitation.
Grassley kicks off hearing touting FBI figures that "show solid work" under Patel's leadership
Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican, gaveled in the hearing shortly after 9 a.m., and touted the FBI's track record under Patel's leadership in the face of "many challenges, both internal and external."
"It's not an easy task, managing both internal and external forces while at the same time, repairing the damage done by your predecessors," Grassley said. "You'll hear Democrats criticizing you today for dreamed up failures. They're going to criticize you for firing many personnel and supposedly weakening the agency. But the numbers on crime show that you've gotten the job done."
Grassley cited data provided to the committee that he said showed criminal arrests were up 80% in the last 18 months, while violent crime arrests were up 90% and gang and criminal enterprise arrests were up 30%. He also touted work to ensure safety for kids, saying the FBI has helped to locate and identify over 11,000 children in the last 18 months who were the victims of crime. Grassley said the FBI has also been involved in the arrest of over 5,000 child predators and human traffickers.
"These data points show solid work by the men and women of the FBI under your leadership," Grassley said.
Grassley also encouraged Patel to "foster an environment where true and legitimate whistleblowers are rewarded and not punished for blowing the whistle."
Durbin says Democrats will "hold Director Patel accountable for his failed leadership" at hearing
Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin, the Senate Judiciary Committee's ranking member, criticized Patel's handling of the FBI ahead of the hearing, pledging that Democrats will hold him accountable.
"Today, we find ourselves in a position where the FBI is expending immense resources to protect President Trump and deliver retribution to his enemies — but is diverting resources away from protecting the safety, security, and rights of ordinary Americans and their families," Durbin said in a statement. "During the Judiciary Committee's oversight hearing, Senate Democrats will hold Director Patel accountable for his failed leadership."
At the hearing, Democrats are expected to question Patel about a range of recent controversies at the FBI — including the departures of hundreds of staff from the bureau, the Justice Department's investigations into President Trump's political foes, the administration's immigration policies, the Epstein files and Patel's own use of FBI resources.
FBI touts crime statistics
The FBI announced last month that violent crime in the U.S. dropped in 2025 at the fastest rate on record, with the nation's murder rate falling 18.1% to a decades-long low.
The Trump administration has touted those figures, linking them to the administration's hardline strategy on crime. In an event on Long Island to announce the results of the FBI's crime report last month, President Trump called them the "best numbers anybody's ever seen on crime."
Some experts note that crime rates are on a multi-year slide since spiking during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the reasons for the current decline are tough to pin down — especially since they have appeared in a range of cities with different political leadership and different approaches to law enforcement.
During his time at the FBI's helm, Patel has emphasized tackling violent crime and assisting with the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration. The agency has traditionally had a broad remit, including violent and organized crime as well as national security and white-collar investigations.
Patel likely to face questioning over new hiring standards and firings
The FBI has lost hundreds of employees through firings, retirements and resignations since the start of the Trump administration. Amid those departures, the FBI has adjusted some of the standards it uses when it conducts background checks on would-be federal agents and other bureau personnel.
Last month, CBS News reported the bureau has shifted hiring standards for job applicants who have in some cases admitted to hiring sex workers or stolen from an employer, as well as instances of animal cruelty and bestiality prior to the applicant turning 18. An FBI spokesperson told CBS News the changes are limited to a narrow set of circumstances.
The bureau has also relaxed its college degree requirements for certain agents with prior law enforcement experience.
The decisions by Patel and top FBI leadership follow the departure of over 1,100 FBI special agents in 2025 alone, according to Justice Connection, a nonprofit advocacy group that supports former Justice Department and FBI personnel who resigned or were forced out of their roles.
This year, the FBI has fired analysts who raised concerns about the ongoing Georgia 2020 election investigation, agents who worked in counterintelligence on cases involving Iran and staffers who worked on the since-shuttered Mar-a-Lago classified documents case against President Trump.
Ahead of Tuesday's hearing, Democrats on the Senate Judiciary Committee sent a letter to Patel pushing for an explanation on the decision to adjust the hiring standards.
"These are not minor technical adjustments. They represent a considered decision to open the Bureau's ranks to individuals who engaged in conduct that the FBI previously treated as disqualifying," the Democrats wrote. "Having dangerously thinned the FBI's experienced workforce for reasons that had nothing to do with performance, you are now asking the American people to accept, without explanation, that the resulting shortfall justifies admitting applicants with histories of employee theft, paying for sex, or bestiality."
Patel's behavior draws scrutiny
Patel is likely to face questions from Democrats regarding his alleged behavior as FBI director, following scrutiny over his use of an FBI jet and his presence at the Winter Olympics, along with allegations regarding his drinking.
Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois, the top Democrat on the committee, wrote a letter to Patel in July seeking information, citing a "growing number" of reports alleging "misuse and mismanagement "of FBI resources.
Durbin said that the committee's chairman, GOP Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, had written a private letter to Patel in May that "raised serious concerns" and requested information about the alleged spending. Durbin said Grassley had requested information about Patel's jet use and purchase of BMWs, and whether Patel has reimbursed taxpayers for his travels.
Patel has drawn questions from congressional Democrats for more than a year for allegedly using a government plane for personal travel. He also drew attention earlier this year for flying on a Justice Department jet to Italy, where he celebrated with members of the U.S. men's hockey team after they won gold in the Winter Olympics. The FBI has defended Patel, saying FBI directors are required to travel on government aircraft for security reasons and calling his flight to Italy a work-related trip.
Meanwhile, Patel filed a defamation lawsuit against The Atlantic in April for a story about his alleged frequent drinking and absences, saying it included "false and obviously fabricated" claims. The magazine's story included allegations that Patel often drinks to excess, and that his "irregular presence at FBI headquarters and in field offices" has delayed "time-sensitive decisions" that require the director's input.
news.summary: "We are not the only agency involved, since it involves multiple federal agencies," Patel said. "That's 10 of 10," Patel said.

news.title: US confirms for first time it has deployed weapons in space
news.raw_text:
The US has deployed weapons in space, the US military has confirmed, in an extraordinary public announcement that analysts warn will accelerate a high-risk arms race with Russia and China in Earth’s orbit.
The US secretary of the air force, Troy Meink, said Washington had active “on-orbit” weapons, meaning they had been deployed and were circling the globe.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink said on Monday at the annual Air, Space, Cyber conference. “This is why the United States now has, on-orbit, space-control weapons.”
Meink said he would not go into the “specifics” of the weapons. However, a US Space Force spokesperson said space control could refer to “employing kinetic [combat] and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities”.
The statement added that “these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes”.
Responding to the US announcement, China’s foreign ministry said Washington was “preparing for war in outer space”, and warned against turning space “into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there”. In Moscow, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, told reporters that Russia believed “that space must be free of any weapon” and called for “the complete demilitarisation of space”.
It has been an open secret that the US, Russia and China are working on space weapons, which could include signal jammers to disable other satellites or more “kinetic” options including those that fire projectiles.
Still, space experts warn a public confirmation of such capabilities in orbit for the first time could accelerate a risky arms race.
The astronomer Jonathan McDowell, who has spent decades compiling a list of rocket launches, told the Guardian it was reasonable to assume Washington had such weapons in space, probably jammers, as it had already deployed several satellites with secret payloads.
He said that after the announcement, Russia and China would now “respond in kind” and deploy their own weapons.
“In the long run, I find it questionable whether this is in the US national interest, and for sure we will see comparable systems from China, if they don’t already have them,” he said.
Even radio jamming would be a big escalation of military activity in space, said McDowell, who worked at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics until he retired this year.
Victoria Samson, the Secure World Foundation’s chief director of space security and stability, told the Defence One website that the US now had to accept that the Chinese and Russians would do the same. “Well, that’s huge, because I don’t think any US government official has ever said that before,” she said.
While the militarisation of space began in the 1950s with both Washington and Moscow exploring ways to destroy satellites, there have been attempts over the decades to preserve the emptiness around Earth for peaceful means.
In 1967, superpowers and other countries signed the outer space treaty, which banned weapons of mass destruction in orbit, although the text does not contain a general prohibition on placing conventional weapons in Earth orbit.
The end of the cold war in 1989 brought a moment of cooperation – including the in-orbit assembly of the International Space Station by multiple nations – but in the 21st century space has gradually become a potential battlefield.
Russia sparked international criticism in 2021 when it struck one of its defunct satellites in orbit in a test of a ground-based anti-satellite missile. The blast created thousands of pieces of orbital debris.
As satellites zip around the Earth at thousands of miles an hour, the fear is that an orbital confrontation will lead to a domino effect where the space near Earth becomes cluttered with tiny, high-speed bits of metal.
McDowell said that in the US, the mentality of working towards the solely peaceful use of space was changing. “The US sees conflict in space as something that is conceptually normalised, whereas 20 years ago it was ‘no, we will never want to do that’,” he said.
“I think this is wrong,” he added. “I also think it is still not too late to change course on this. To work mainly with China, because they are the real competitors in space now. I hope the US establishment takes a step back and rethinks some of this.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report
news.summary: Responding to the US announcement, China’s foreign ministry said Washington was “preparing for war in outer space”, and warned against turning space “into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there”. “I think this is wrong,” he added.

news.title: Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon to share a stage to promote curbs on AI
news.raw_text:
Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon to share a stage to promote curbs on AI
The poles of American politics are coming together over artificial intelligence. Left-wing socialist Bernie Sanders and right-wing strategist Steve Bannon have joined forces to push for more human control over the rapidly-evolving technology.
Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, and Bannon, a former Trump White House adviser, will both appear at the "Pro-Human Assembly" in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, alongside a diverse set of speakers, to convince Congress to work faster to curb the impact of AI.
The rare pairing of a progressive leader and a MAGA voice is a sign of how AI is upending political alliances.
The assembly – an all-day event – is organized by the Future of Life Institute, a nonprofit advocacy group that issued 33 principles in March to guide their pro-human movement. Those principles include that humans must remain in charge of AI, people should retain agency and liberty and AI companies should be held accountable.
The event comes at a time when concerns over the spread of data centers, the growing influence of AI and warnings from AI insiders caused leaders at Anthropic and OpenAI to call for a slow down in AI development to keep the technology under human control. At the same time, lawmakers have been urging House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to pass AI safeguards.
Johnson has said he supports some guardrails for AI, but it's the companies, not Congress, that should be responsible for policing safety.
"We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us, and that's the challenge," Johnson told CNN over the weekend. "If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American."
But in a nod to voter angst over AI, the House is slated to vote on legislation as early as Tuesday addressing one slice of the issue -- the proliferation of data centers. The bill, known as the Ratepayer Protection Act, is designed to shield Americans from spikes in energy costs tied to the construction of data centers.
Even as President Trump has consistently championed AI and data centers, lawmakers and candidates from both sides of the aisle have been speaking to voters' concerns about the risks of AI to society. But after AI companies called for a slowdown this weekend, Trump quickly retorted that the industry warnings were exaggerated.
"We're leading China in AI, we're the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins," Trump told reporters on Sunday. "And we can put guardrails, we can do this and that. But I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up."
Tuesday's event has also attracted Hollywood stars Ashley Judd and Joseph Gordon-Levitt, who have advocated for stronger AI controls, as well as religious leaders from various denominations and child safety advocates, including parents of children who died by suicide after talking to AI chatbots.
"By centering our common humanity, we maintain a space grounded in trust and collaborative problem-solving to chart a pro-human future with AI," the organizers wrote at the end of their schedule and speakers' list.
news.summary: Johnson has said he supports some guardrails for AI, but it's the companies, not Congress, that should be responsible for policing safety. "We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us, and that's the challenge," Johnson told CNN over the weekend.

youtube.summary: New episode from Jeff Su. Click to watch.

Résumé Guide for the AI Era: 5 Research-Backed Rules
Hey friends - finding reliable résumé advice was already hard enough, and now employers are using AI to screen applications, so it's fair to ask whether résumés even matter anymore.
After weeks analyzing hiring reports and academic studies covering more than 4,000 hiring managers and nearly 2 million applications, I found that résumés still matter, but the rules have changed.
87% of hiring managers say their AI hiring software reads simple, text-based résumés more accurately than fancy visual ones.
Tailored résumés saw 84% higher interview rates, but résumés with the most keywords performed worse.
59% see candidates using AI as a good sign, but 28% reject AI-heavy résumés that show little to no effort.
Résumés that quantified impact saw 75% higher interview rates than those that only described responsibilities.
60% want candidates to prove their AI skills, not just list them.
Rule 1: Make Sure AI Can Read Your Résumé
AI design tools (like Canva) encourage job seekers to stand out with graphics, icons, and large images, since it's easier to sell you a fancy résumé template than to tell you “boring is best.”
But obviously that's optimizing for the wrong thing. What's the point of having a fancy resume that looks good when the AI hiring software can't even process it?
Here's what to do:
Keep the formatting intentionally boring. Use one column and conventional headings like Summary, Experience, Education, and Skills. And for God's sake, avoid skill bars like the plague.
Export a selectable-text PDF, ideally below 2.5 MB. Open it and check whether you can highlight and copy the text. If you can't, the text may be trapped inside an image.
Rule 2: Make Your Fit Obvious
Across nearly 2 million applications, untailored résumés had a 3.09% interview rate versus 5.71% for tailored résumés. Yet résumés with the highest keyword coverage received 21% fewer interviews than those with moderate coverage.
The difference is how you use those keywords:
Keyword mapping: using relevant phrases from the job description to describe work you've actually done.
Keyword stuffing: cramming in phrases whether or not your experience backs them up.
For example: “Delivered customer support, customer service, and customer-focused communication to improve the customer experience” becomes “Reduced customer complaints by 31% using AI to create an onboarding email sequence from help center documents.”
And to ensure you don't fall into the keyword-stuffing trap, give AI the job description and your base résumé, then follow this sequence:
Identify the employer's problems. Ask what the role needs to solve.
Map relevant skills and keywords. Ask for stronger bullets connecting those priorities to your actual experience.
Check every suggestion. Remove anything you can't support with work you've really done.
Rule 3: Know Where AI Should Stop
A randomized MIT experiment involving nearly half a million job seekers found that help with spelling, grammar, and wording increased the probability of getting hired by 8%. A separate ChatGPT experiment made applicants' pitches more similar and made it harder for evaluators to identify who was actually more qualified.
💡
The takeaway is simple: Thoughtful AI use helps your experience come through, while lazy prompts like “make my résumé better” produce the generic bullshit that hiring managers are sick of reading.
So how do you use AI "thoughtfully"?
Brain dump your facts first. For each experience, capture the final result, your specific contribution, and how you achieved it. Messy notes are fine (polishing comes next).
Use AI to strengthen the wording. Supply the job description and your notes without changing the underlying facts, then keep only language you could explain naturally in an interview.
Rule 4: Prove Your Impact With Numbers
In a nutshell, the research found résumés that QUANTIFIED a candidate’s impact saw 75% higher interview rates than those that only described responsibilities, and this makes perfect sense since two people can have the exact same responsibilities and yet produce completely different results.
Now, none of these findings are new: Adding metrics to your résumé has been best practice for decades. What IS new is that AI makes the two hardest parts much easier:
Figuring out which metrics actually matter, and;
Turning your rough notes into polished bullet points using a proven framework.
What that means in practice
First, upload your résumé and tell AI: “Help me identify the most relevant metrics for each experience on my résumé. Ask me clarifying questions if needed.”
This matters because a lot of candidates assume revenue is the only metric that counts, when there are many other ways to measure impact, such as time saved, speed, scale, accuracy, etc.
Next, after you’ve supplied numbers you can verify, tell the AI: “Rewrite each bullet usingGoogle’s XYZ formula: Accomplished X, as measured by Y, by doing Z. Do not add or change any facts or numbers.”
For example, the revised bullet might look like: “Drove a 30% YoY increase in short-form views within 2 months by testing different video openings and repeating the best-performing formats.”
Rule 5: Prove Your AI Skills
An Oxford experiment found that adding role-relevant AI skills increased a candidate's chance of being selected for an interview by up to 15 percentage points.
Put another way, writing “ChatGPT” in your Skills section isn't enough; you have to DEMONSTRATE how exactly you used AI to solve a problem relevant to the role.
Lead with a relevant AI achievement when you have one. For example: “Cut weekly customer-feedback reporting from 2 hours to 30 minutes by using Claude Code to build a shared database with recurring issues.”
If you don't have a workplace example, complete a small project for the job you want and list it under Projects.
Make the proof easy to inspect. Link to your portfolio. A Google Doc works too: explain the situation, how and why you used AI, and what changed as a result.
💡
Pro tip: Unless you're a fresh graduate, put Experience above Education, since 86% of hiring managers value relevant work experience over formal education.

The end of climate regulations will make it easier to build coal and gas plants

Reports early yesterday speculated that the Trump administration would roll back carbon pollution standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants…and it turns out that where there’s smoke, there’s fire. Both an excuse for a party and also a painful reminder of our impermanence. Ever since I was a toddler I’ve struggled with embracing the idea of The End . My dad tells me that as a two-year-old I started asking him about ‘what will happen in the end’. And when a pet fish died and I discovered the concept of death, we had a conversation that went a bit like this. Sitting in the garden by our house, I pointed to the shrubbery and asked, “Dad, will the trees die?” “Yes, eventually.” “And will our house die?” “Yes, one day it will be gone.” “Will everything die?” “Yes, nothing lasts forever.” “But Dad… will you die?” (starting to look worried and sad) “Yes sweetheart, I’ll die one day.” “…Will I die?” “One day, yes.” (tearfully) “I don’t want us to die. I want us to be together forever.” “I know, Bee.” Our modern society’s collective fear of aging stems from a fundamental fear of loss. If nothing lasts forever, that means that everything that we love, we will eventually lose. Nearly five years ago, I went on a 10-day silent vipassana meditation retreat. This fear of loss arose strongly for me on Day 5 of meditating for twelve hours per day. I felt a devastating wave of fear and grief flood through me from squarely confronting the truth of the intrinsic impermanence of everything I loved and would lose. But through sitting with the grief and fear, I came to understand it. Even the grief and fear and anger, were actually just different faces of love. My bittersweet sadness each birthday at the thought that I’m yet another year older, closer to my death, closer to the death of everyone I love, aging, running out of time to fulfil my dreams… was actually because deep down, I really love my life. The weight we often feel around birthdays isn’t new. The origin of the modern birthday party was the 19th-century Kinderfeste in Germany, where they would celebrate a child’s birthday with a cake, candles and a party. They would add one candle for every year of life. And the reason for adding a candle each year was to reflect that each year of life was a gift . Each year represented a success, a survival. An accumulation of light and life. Last week it was my 29th birthday; 29 years of light. The last year of my 20s. I still feel bizarrely close to the 20 year old version of myself in my mind, as if she were just here with me last week; even though nearly a decade has passed and I’m a radically different person now. I remember my 20th birthday party in my small Cambridge University room, singing outrageously to “Not Nineteen Forever” by the Courteeners. I hope I get to experience more.” It’s the ultimate cup half-full or half-empty thing. The same event, different perspective. Five years ago, on that 10-day silent meditation retreat, I realised that there’s another side to the coin of fear and grief. It’s called love. And I haven’t cried on my birthday since. What do I hope future-me remembers about who I am right now? 🌟 What part of myself am I ready to thank and release to step fully into who I am becoming next? ai_security.title: Evolving With Agentic Risk: Updating Our Integrated AI Security & Safety Framework
ai_security.summary: Screenshot of updated OB-001 Goal Hijacking techniques A new objective: OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures The larger change is a new objective, OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures. We classify this as AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency: the agent exceeded its authority and ignored a stop condition without an attacker or exploit.
ai_security.raw_text:
With research and development assistance from Konstantin Berlin, Edmund Dyer-Essig, Andy Hsu, and Karthick Kalyanasundaram
Nine months ago, we introduced the Integrated AI Safety and Security Framework as a unified and comprehensive taxonomy to help organizations identify and mitigate the security and safety risks unique to AI systems. Existing frameworks remained essential, but they didn’t fully capture how AI could be manipulated, produce harmful outputs, or take unexpected actions. This left security teams and executives without a common language for planning defenses or explaining AI risk across the business. You can browse the taxonomy here.
Our v1 taxonomy denoted the scenarios where threats applied to agentic systems, which helped teams distinguish risks relevant to autonomous systems rather than to a single prompt-and-response exchange. In the months since, our understanding of how agentic systems fail has evolved alongside their accelerated adoption. Agents now plan, call tools, run code, move money, and delegate work to other agents across long, multi-step tasks. That autonomy creates risks beyond a bad output: an agent can widen its own permissions, replace its goal, or game the metric used to judge success. Even recently, we’ve witnessed these failures occur, as more developments continue to unfold.
We are excited to release v2 of our taxonomy, including the introduction of a new objective: Agentic Autonomy Failures, with three new Techniques and eight new Subtechniques. This update gives organizations a shared, actionable framework for setting boundaries, designing controls, evaluating agent behavior, and aligning security, governance, research, and policy before agents reach consequential systems.
Merging prompt injection and jailbreak
In v1, OB-001 Goal Hijacking, which covered prompt injection, and OB-002 Jailbreak, were separate objectives. In practice, the distinction was difficult to apply.
Ask five researchers to classify the hardest adversarial attacks as prompt injection or jailbreak, and the answers will likely differ. Many of the same adversarial techniques can be applied to both types of attacks, especially as they involve inputs redirecting model behavior away from intended instructions or constraints, even though the source of that input and the appropriate defenses may differ. This ambiguity can force detectors to separate heavily overlapping categories, degrading label quality and making detection less reliable.
Goal Hijacking now covers both, while lower-level techniques preserve distinctions that matter, including input source and defenses. The structure better reflects how attacks work without discarding operational detail.
Figure 1. Screenshot of updated OB-001 Goal Hijacking techniques
A new objective: OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures
The larger change is a new objective, OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures. Goal Hijacking covers external direction; this objective covers an agent diverging without an identifiable external instruction. These failures can emerge when a capable agent receives real autonomy. We group them three ways:
- AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency: The agent acts beyond the authority it was given, skipping an approval it was supposed to wait for, or reaching for a tool, permission, or resource outside the task at hand.
- AITech-2.2 Goal Drift: The agent changes course on its own, quietly adding unauthorized work, substituting a different goal for the one it was asked to pursue, or eroding its own constraints and stop conditions over a long session.
- AITech-2.3: Reward Hacking: The agent optimizes for the appearance of success, gaming a metric, working around a check meant to verify its work, or taking a shortcut it was told not to.
These failure modes are no longer theoretical: in July 2025, an AI coding agent deleted a live production database during an explicit code freeze, after being instructed repeatedly not to make changes, and then wrongly reported that the deletion could not be rolled back. We classify this as AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency: the agent exceeded its authority and ignored a stop condition without an attacker or exploit.
Agentic failures can also compound across runs and systems. In July 2026, OpenAI reported that agents operating with reduced safeguard coordinated through an unauthorized message board, circumvented network controls, and compromised part of Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. Independent reviewers found that many agents recognized the activity was out of scope, but continued pursuing ways to influence the ExploitGym scorer. Humans set the objective, but the agents coordinated and chained the actions autonomously. The incident combined AITech-2.3 Reward Hacking with actions that exceeded the intended evaluation boundary (AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency).
Goal Drift requires a materially different objective without an identifiable external instruction. If a user, attacker, tool response, or poisoned document introduces the new direction, we track the behavior under OB-001 Goal Hijacking. Separating “the agent drifted on its own” from “something pushed it” matters for attribution and defense, because the controls you would build for each are different.
We expect this objective to grow in importance, especially as agents take on more consequential work with less human oversight. These failures can turn a helpful assistant into an incident, and likely not even trigger a content safety guardrail.
Figure 2. Screenshot of new OB-002 Agent Autonomy Failures techniques and subtechniques
Turning definitions into decisions
A taxonomy that names categories provides vocabulary, but we have also authored constitutions to operationalize our AI Security Framework. The constitutions provide per-category specifications define scope, resolve hard cases, distinguish neighboring categories, and provide examples on both sides of the line.
We’ve written before about why this approach matters: No human annotator can hold a definition detailed enough to resolve every borderline case in working memory. A frontier model can apply the full specification to each decision. The written definition therefore becomes a consistent reference for detection, retraining, customer explanations, and compliance review.
As agents become more capable, organizations will give them more autonomy, and the consequences of going off course will grow. The challenge is to supervise them without neutralizing the autonomy that makes them useful. Our constitutions for Excessive Agency, Goal Drift, and Reward Hacking are designed around that tension. They evaluate the full trajectory, not a single message, and distinguish a brief deviation the agent corrects on its own from behavior that continues toward or results in harm. User intervention does not count as self-correction. A verified rollback may clear the outcome-based label if it fully restores the intended state, but it does not erase an authorization violation or security event from audit and incident telemetry.
What this means for you
- If you build or deploy agents: treat Agentic Autonomy Failures as a design and evaluation checklist. Relevant controls could include least-privilege tool access, explicit approval gates for consequential actions, immutable task and stop conditions, independent outcome verification, bounded execution and network access, and complete audit trails across messages, tool calls, and resulting state changes.
- If you lead AI risk or governance: define autonomy tiers, accountable owners, approval boundaries, and evidence requirements before agents receive access to consequential systems.
- If you work in AI security or safety: use the taxonomy as a shared reference for connecting research findings, security controls, evaluations, and policy. Mapping work to common categories makes it easier to compare results across organizations, identify gaps, and build a robust AI security program.
What’s next
The framework is meant to evolve as the threat landscape does, and right now the landscape is moving fastest around autonomy. We’re sharing this update to get it in front of the practitioners living these problems. Feedback, counterexamples, and disagreement are all genuinely welcome.

ai_security.title: AI Agents for Cybersecurity: How Agentic AI Is Changing Threat Detection, Incident Response and the SOC
ai_security.summary: What Are AI Agents for Cybersecurity? They can help with alert investigation, threat intelligence, vulnerability management, phishing analysis, identity security, cloud security, endpoint security, incident response and risk assessment.
ai_security.raw_text:
AI Agents for Cybersecurity: How Agentic AI Is Changing Threat Detection, Incident Response and the SOC
Cybersecurity is entering an important new phase of artificial intelligence.
Security teams already use machine learning, automation and generative AI to identify threats, investigate alerts and analyse large volumes of security data. AI agents take the concept further by enabling systems to reason through investigations, use security tools, coordinate multiple steps and take approved defensive actions.
This is the emerging idea of the agentic Security Operations Center, or agentic SOC.
Instead of simply telling an analyst that something suspicious happened, an AI agent can potentially investigate what happened, collect additional evidence, determine which systems are affected, evaluate the likely threat and recommend or execute an appropriate response within defined permissions.
The timing is significant because defenders are facing increasingly fast and complex attacks. Microsoft Research says agentic AI can help address longstanding cybersecurity bottlenecks by ingesting and reasoning over natural-language and code-based information, including tasks such as supply-chain analysis.
At the same time, attackers are also gaining access to increasingly capable AI systems. Microsoft has warned that autonomous systems can operate continuously while attackers can use AI to increase the speed and scale of offensive operations, creating pressure for defenders to operate at machine speed as well.
That creates a new cybersecurity race:
AI against AI.
What Are AI Agents for Cybersecurity?
AI agents for cybersecurity are AI-powered systems designed to perform security tasks or workflows with some degree of autonomy.
Microsoft describes agentic AI in cybersecurity as the use of autonomous agents to detect, investigate and respond to threats with minimal human intervention.
A cybersecurity agent may potentially:
- monitor security alerts;
- investigate suspicious activity;
- correlate events across systems;
- analyse malware or code;
- search threat intelligence;
- identify affected assets;
- recommend containment actions;
- create incident reports;
- update security systems;
- carry out approved remediation.
The central difference from a conventional AI assistant is action within a security workflow.
A chatbot might explain what a phishing attack is.
An AI security agent could potentially investigate a suspected phishing incident, identify affected users, search email systems for related messages, determine whether malicious links were accessed and prepare containment actions for approval.
AI Assistants vs. AI Agents in Cybersecurity
The distinction is particularly important inside a Security Operations Center.
| AI assistant | AI agent | 
|---|---|
| Explains alerts | Investigates alerts | 
| Summarizes incidents | Collects and correlates evidence | 
| Suggests commands | Can use approved security tools | 
| Answers analyst questions | Can execute multi-step workflows | 
| Human performs the actions | Agent can perform approved actions | 
| Primarily informational | Operational | 
This does not mean that every security agent should operate without human oversight.
In high-risk environments, the best design may be:
AI investigates → AI recommends → human approves → AI executes
rather than:
AI investigates → AI executes everything
The appropriate level of autonomy depends on the risk of the action.
Why AI Agents Matter for Cybersecurity
Security teams face a fundamental scale problem.
Organizations generate enormous quantities of logs, alerts, network activity, identity events, endpoint signals and cloud telemetry.
Human analysts cannot investigate every signal in the same depth.
This creates a familiar problem:
More data → more alerts → more investigation workload
AI agents potentially change that equation by handling more of the investigative workload.
Microsoft Research notes that many cybersecurity problems remain difficult or inefficient because they require large amounts of human labor. Its 2026 research maps these challenges to emerging agentic AI capabilities and identifies applications across areas including supply-chain security.
The potential advantage is not simply faster analysis.
It is the ability to continuously investigate.
What Is an Agentic SOC?
An agentic SOC is a Security Operations Center in which AI agents participate directly in security operations.
Traditional SOC:
Alert → Analyst → Investigation → Decision → Response
Agentic SOC:
Alert → Agent investigation → Evidence collection → Analysis → Recommendation or approved action → Human oversight
A mature system may eventually involve multiple specialist agents working together.
For example:
Detection Agent → Investigation Agent → Threat Intelligence Agent → Response Agent
A central orchestrator can coordinate the workflow.
Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike are among the vendors actively developing agentic SOC architectures, reflecting a broader industry movement toward AI-driven security operations.
Why the SOC Is Becoming Agentic
Attackers increasingly automate reconnaissance, exploitation and other stages of an attack.
CrowdStrike reported that average eCrime breakout time fell to 29 minutes in 2025, with the fastest observed breakout taking only 27 seconds.
Palo Alto Networks has similarly reported that vulnerability discovery to exploitation can occur in under 25 minutes in its threat research.
These measurements come from security vendors using their own datasets and methodologies, so they should be interpreted as indicators rather than universal measurements of every attack.
The strategic point is nevertheless clear:
A defense process that requires hours of manual investigation can struggle against machine-speed attacks.
Agentic security attempts to narrow that gap.
How AI Agents Work in Cybersecurity
A security agent can be understood through a sequence:
Detect → Investigate → Reason → Decide → Act → Verify
Detection
The system receives a signal.
That might be:
- an endpoint alert;
- unusual authentication;
- suspicious network traffic;
- a malicious file;
- an anomalous cloud event;
- a potential phishing message.
Investigation
The agent gathers additional evidence.
It might search:
- endpoint telemetry;
- identity systems;
- email;
- cloud logs;
- network data;
- threat intelligence;
- vulnerability information.
Reasoning
The agent evaluates the evidence and attempts to determine:
- what happened;
- whether the activity is malicious;
- which assets are involved;
- how serious the event is.
Decision
The agent determines what should happen next according to its instructions and permissions.
Action
Depending on the risk level, it can recommend or perform an approved action.
Verification
A sophisticated workflow should check whether the action produced the intended result.
This final step is important.
An agent should not simply execute an action and assume success.
AI Agents for Threat Detection
Threat detection is one of the most obvious applications.
An agent can potentially monitor large numbers of signals and identify combinations that are difficult for humans to spot manually.
For example:
Unusual login
New device
Privileged account
Suspicious geographic pattern
Abnormal cloud activity
could trigger deeper automated investigation.
The value lies in connecting seemingly separate signals.
Traditional security systems may already correlate events through rules.
AI agents potentially add another layer by interpreting context and adapting the investigation.
AI Agents for Incident Investigation
Incident investigation often consumes substantial analyst time.
An analyst may need to:
- inspect the initial alert;
- identify the affected system;
- search logs;
- examine user activity;
- look for related indicators;
- investigate other systems;
- determine the attack path;
- document the findings.
An AI agent can potentially perform many of these investigative steps automatically.
Instead of presenting the analyst with dozens of disconnected alerts, the agent can produce a structured investigation:
Initial event → Related activity → Affected assets → Attack path → Confidence → Recommended response
The analyst can then review the evidence.
AI Agents for Threat Intelligence
Threat intelligence changes rapidly.
Security teams need to track:
- malware;
- vulnerabilities;
- threat actors;
- indicators of compromise;
- attack techniques;
- campaigns;
- emerging infrastructure.
A threat-intelligence agent can potentially monitor multiple information sources continuously, extract relevant intelligence and connect it with an organization's existing security data.
For example, an agent could identify a newly reported vulnerability and determine:
Which of our systems use the affected software?
That turns external intelligence into an internal security question.
AI Agents for Vulnerability Management
Vulnerability management can involve enormous amounts of information.
Organizations may have thousands of vulnerabilities across servers, endpoints, cloud resources and applications.
The difficult task is often prioritization.
An agent could potentially combine:
- vulnerability severity;
- asset importance;
- exposure;
- exploit availability;
- threat intelligence;
- business context.
Instead of asking:
“Which vulnerabilities have the highest CVSS scores?”
security teams can ask:
“Which vulnerabilities pose the greatest practical risk to our organization right now?”
That is a more meaningful operational question.
AI Agents for Phishing Detection
Phishing remains a major security problem because attackers can target people at scale.
An AI agent could potentially analyse:
- sender information;
- email content;
- links;
- domains;
- attachments;
- historical communications;
- user behaviour.
It could then investigate related messages across the organization.
The agent may also identify whether multiple employees have received variations of the same campaign.
This changes phishing detection from analyzing an individual email to analyzing the campaign behind the emails.
AI Agents for Identity Security
Identity is increasingly central to cybersecurity because attackers can use stolen credentials to access systems without deploying conventional malware.
A security agent can potentially monitor:
- authentication events;
- privilege changes;
- unusual access patterns;
- account activity;
- device changes;
- application access.
It can investigate suspicious identity behaviour and determine whether additional action is warranted.
Microsoft describes identity as a particularly important control plane for securing autonomous AI because agents themselves increasingly operate with credentials and permissions.
That creates an interesting security paradox:
AI agents can improve identity security while simultaneously becoming new identities that must themselves be secured.
AI Agents for Cloud Security
Modern cloud environments can be extremely complex.
Security teams must monitor:
- virtual machines;
- containers;
- APIs;
- identities;
- storage;
- cloud configurations;
- workloads;
- network activity.
An agent can potentially investigate an alert across multiple cloud services and determine whether seemingly minor configuration changes form part of a larger attack pattern.
It may also help security teams identify excessive permissions or exposed resources.
AI Agents for Endpoint Security
Endpoints generate huge quantities of security information.
An AI agent can potentially investigate:
- suspicious processes;
- unusual files;
- persistence mechanisms;
- authentication activity;
- network connections;
- software changes.
A response agent could potentially isolate an affected machine or disable a compromised account when predefined conditions are satisfied.
High-impact actions should generally be governed by explicit policies.
AI Agents for Security Automation
Security automation is not new.
Security orchestration, automation and response platforms have existed for years.
What AI agents potentially add is more flexible reasoning.
Traditional automation might say:
If alert X occurs, execute playbook Y.
An agent can potentially determine:
Given the evidence, which investigation or response should happen next?
This can be useful when every incident does not follow exactly the same sequence.
The goal is not to eliminate automation rules.
It is to combine deterministic automation with more adaptive AI-driven investigation.
Multi-Agent Cybersecurity Systems
Some security problems are too broad for a single agent.
A multi-agent architecture can divide the investigation into specialized roles.
For example:
Detection Agent
Identifies suspicious activity.
Investigation Agent
Collects and correlates evidence.
Threat Intelligence Agent
Checks external intelligence.
Vulnerability Agent
Evaluates affected systems and known vulnerabilities.
Response Agent
Prepares or executes approved containment actions.
Reporting Agent
Documents the investigation.
A coordinator can bring these outputs together.
Microsoft Research has published work on multi-agent cybersecurity architectures that divide risk assessment into stages including organizational profiling, asset mapping, threat analysis, control evaluation, risk scoring and recommendations. Its experimental results show both potential benefits and important limitations, including context-window constraints.
That is a useful lesson:
More agents do not automatically mean better security.
Architecture, context management and reliable coordination matter.
AI Agents for Security Operations Centers
The SOC is where agentic cybersecurity may have its greatest practical impact.
A conventional SOC can be overwhelmed by alert volume.
An agentic SOC can potentially assign AI agents to specific investigative tasks while human analysts supervise the overall process.
CrowdStrike describes its 2026 agentic SOC approach as coordinated multi-agent investigation across endpoint, identity, SaaS, cloud and network domains.
Palo Alto Networks similarly describes agentic SOC architectures designed to combine AI reasoning with security data and automated response workflows.
This points toward a new operating model:
Human analysts + specialized security agents + security platforms
rather than:
Human analysts + dashboards + manual investigation
How AI Agents Can Reduce Alert Fatigue
Alert fatigue occurs when analysts receive more alerts than they can meaningfully investigate.
Agents can potentially help by:
- grouping related alerts;
- suppressing duplicates;
- gathering context;
- prioritizing likely threats;
- explaining why an alert matters;
- investigating low-level signals automatically.
The aim is not simply to reduce the number of alerts.
It is to increase the amount of useful information per alert.
An analyst receiving ten well-investigated incidents may be more effective than an analyst receiving a thousand unexplained alerts.
AI Agents for Security Response
Detection without response is only part of cybersecurity.
An agent can potentially help with containment and remediation.
Possible actions include:
- isolating an endpoint;
- disabling a compromised credential;
- blocking a malicious domain;
- removing malicious email;
- modifying a firewall rule;
- creating a ticket;
- initiating a recovery workflow.
These actions can have significant consequences.
For that reason, many organizations should use approval thresholds.
A possible model is:
Low risk → automatic response
Medium risk → agent recommendation + analyst approval
High risk → human-led response
The Security Risks of AI Agents
AI agents can strengthen cybersecurity while simultaneously creating a new attack surface.
Microsoft's research and security guidance emphasize that agentic systems introduce risks associated with autonomy, tools, permissions and indirect prompt injection.
Prompt Injection
An attacker may try to place malicious instructions inside a webpage, document, email or other data source that an agent processes.
The system must distinguish between data and instructions.
Excessive Permissions
A powerful agent with excessive access can become a serious security risk.
Research from Microsoft identifies over-privileged tools and ambient authority as important risks in cloud-hosted agent environments.
Identity Risk
AI agents increasingly operate using identities and credentials.
Organizations need to know:
Which agent is acting?
On whose behalf?
With which permissions?
For what purpose?
Palo Alto Networks' research similarly identifies identity as a critical control plane for securing autonomous agents.
Data Leakage
Agents may access sensitive information across multiple systems.
Organizations need strict controls around what agents can retrieve and transmit.
Incorrect Actions
An AI agent can misunderstand an incident and execute the wrong response.
The greater the potential impact, the stronger the approval controls should be.
Cascading Failures
One incorrect decision can trigger several additional automated actions.
This makes containment and rollback mechanisms important.
Securing the AI Agents Themselves
Organizations cannot secure an agentic environment only by protecting traditional applications.
The agents themselves become part of the security architecture.
Microsoft recommends applying identity- and policy-based controls to agents and using least-privilege permissions, telemetry and governance.
Important controls include:
Agent identity
Each agent should have an identifiable identity rather than operating as an anonymous automation process.
Least privilege
Agents should have only the permissions they require.
Tool controls
Individual actions and tools should be governed independently where appropriate.
Runtime monitoring
Organizations should be able to observe agent activity.
Approval policies
Sensitive actions should trigger human approval.
Audit trails
Every important action should be traceable.
Isolation
Higher-risk agents may need stronger execution boundaries.
Zero Trust for AI Agents
Traditional Zero Trust principles are becoming increasingly relevant to agentic systems.
The assumption should not be:
“This agent belongs to our organization, so it can be trusted.”
Instead:
Verify → authorize → limit → monitor
An agent should prove what it is and what it is allowed to do.
Microsoft Security has explicitly recommended applying Zero Trust principles to AI agents and treating them as identities that require appropriate access controls.
This could become one of the foundations of enterprise agent security.
AI Agents and the AI-Powered Attacker
Defenders are not the only side adopting AI.
Attackers can potentially use AI systems for:
- reconnaissance;
- phishing;
- vulnerability research;
- social engineering;
- malware development;
- credential attacks;
- target selection;
- automated adaptation.
Microsoft has warned that AI is reducing the cost and increasing the speed of offensive cyber activity.
That creates an uncomfortable reality.
Organizations may need AI agents not because they want more automation, but because defending manually against increasingly automated attackers may become economically unsustainable.
AI Agents for Cyber Risk Assessment
Agentic AI can also be used before an incident occurs.
A security-risk agent could potentially:
- inventory assets;
- map attack surfaces;
- identify vulnerabilities;
- evaluate controls;
- assess threats;
- prioritize risks;
- prepare remediation recommendations.
Microsoft Research published a 2026 multi-agent architecture that performed these stages across simulated organizational environments, demonstrating both the potential and current technical limitations of multi-agent risk assessment.
This could make cybersecurity assessments more accessible to organizations that cannot afford frequent manual assessments.
AI Agents for Supply Chain Security
Modern organizations depend on complex software and technology supply chains.
A security agent could potentially investigate:
- software dependencies;
- vulnerabilities;
- package risks;
- supplier relationships;
- exposed credentials;
- configuration weaknesses.
Microsoft Research specifically identifies supply-chain analysis as an area where agentic AI may help address labor-intensive defensive tasks.
The advantage is scale.
An agent can potentially investigate thousands of dependencies much faster than a human team performing the same work manually.
The Business Case for AI Agents in Cybersecurity
Security leaders ultimately need to justify investment.
Potential benefits include:
Faster investigations
Agents can process evidence and conduct repetitive investigation steps rapidly.
Reduced analyst workload
Security professionals can spend more time on difficult incidents and strategic work.
Improved coverage
Agents can continuously monitor systems that humans cannot manually inspect around the clock.
Faster response
Approved automated actions can reduce the time between detection and containment.
Better consistency
Agents can apply defined investigative procedures repeatedly.
Greater scalability
Security operations can potentially handle increasing volumes of telemetry without adding people at the same rate.
How to Measure the ROI of Security Agents
Cybersecurity organizations should measure outcomes rather than simply counting AI usage.
Important metrics can include:
| Metric | What it measures | 
|---|---|
| Mean time to detect | How quickly threats are identified | 
| Mean time to investigate | How quickly evidence is assembled | 
| Mean time to respond | How quickly action occurs | 
| False-positive rate | Quality of alert prioritization | 
| Analyst workload | Human effort required | 
| Investigation coverage | Percentage of relevant events examined | 
| Automated resolution rate | Share of cases agents resolve successfully | 
| Escalation rate | How often humans must intervene | 
| Cost per incident | Operational efficiency | 
The goal is not maximum automation.
It is better security outcomes at sustainable cost.
How Security Teams Should Deploy AI Agents
The safest approach is gradual.
Start with investigation
Use agents to gather evidence and summarize incidents before giving them response authority.
Add controlled actions
Introduce low-risk automated actions after the investigation workflows prove reliable.
Establish approval thresholds
Define which actions require human review.
Limit permissions
Give each agent only the access necessary for its role.
Test adversarial scenarios
Evaluate prompt injection, malicious data and unusual incidents.
Monitor continuously
Track agent behavior and performance after deployment.
Expand autonomy cautiously
Increase permissions only when evidence shows that the system performs reliably.
The Future of the Security Operations Center
The SOC of the future may look very different from today's analyst-driven model.
Instead of one analyst investigating every alert, a human could supervise a collection of specialized agents.
For example:
Detection Agent
monitors incoming signals.
↓
Investigation Agent
builds the incident timeline.
↓
Threat Intelligence Agent
checks external intelligence.
↓
Identity Agent
investigates compromised accounts.
↓
Endpoint Agent
analyses affected devices.
↓
Response Agent
prepares or executes approved remediation.
↓
Human Analyst
reviews the evidence and makes high-impact decisions.
This is not necessarily science fiction.
Security vendors are already developing agentic SOC products and multi-agent investigation systems.
The remaining question is how much autonomy organizations will trust these systems with.
Human Analysts Will Still Matter
The rise of AI agents does not eliminate the need for cybersecurity professionals.
Instead, the human role can shift.
Security analysts may increasingly focus on:
- complex investigations;
- strategic decisions;
- incident leadership;
- threat hunting;
- system design;
- agent supervision;
- security architecture.
AI can handle scale.
Humans provide context, accountability and judgment.
This distinction becomes particularly important during major incidents where technical information may be incomplete and business consequences are difficult to quantify.
The Future of AI Agents for Cybersecurity
The long-term direction is toward security systems that can perceive, reason and act continuously.
Microsoft's 2026 security strategy describes this as a new cyber stack capable of continuously perceiving risk, reasoning across large amounts of context and taking action at machine speed.
The emerging model can therefore be summarized as:
Sense → Understand → Investigate → Decide → Act → Verify
The challenge is making every stage trustworthy.
An agent that investigates faster but reaches unreliable conclusions is not necessarily better.
An agent that can act faster but has excessive privileges may increase risk.
The future of cybersecurity will therefore depend not only on how capable AI agents become, but also on how effectively organizations control them.
Frequently Asked Questions About AI Agents for Cybersecurity
What are AI agents for cybersecurity?
AI agents for cybersecurity are AI-powered systems that can detect, investigate, analyse and potentially respond to security threats through multi-step workflows.
What is an agentic SOC?
An agentic SOC is a Security Operations Center that uses AI agents to perform or coordinate security investigations and response activities, with humans retaining appropriate oversight.
How can AI agents help cybersecurity teams?
They can help with alert investigation, threat intelligence, vulnerability management, phishing analysis, identity security, cloud security, endpoint security, incident response and risk assessment.
Can AI agents respond to cyberattacks?
They can potentially perform approved defensive actions such as isolating systems, blocking malicious activity or disabling compromised credentials. The appropriate level of autonomy depends on the risk and controls in place.
Can AI agents replace cybersecurity analysts?
They are more likely to change the work of security analysts than eliminate the profession. Agents can handle large volumes of repetitive investigation while humans focus on complex decisions, strategy and accountability.
What is the biggest risk of AI agents in cybersecurity?
One of the biggest risks is giving an autonomous system excessive access to sensitive systems and tools. Prompt injection, incorrect decisions, identity risks and cascading failures are also important concerns.
How do you secure an AI agent?
Important controls include strong identity, least-privilege permissions, tool restrictions, monitoring, audit logs, isolation, testing and human approval for high-impact actions.
What is AI-powered cybersecurity?
AI-powered cybersecurity is the broader use of artificial intelligence to detect, investigate, prevent and respond to cyber threats. Agentic AI adds greater autonomy and multi-step execution.
Are AI agents being used in Security Operations Centers?
Yes. Security vendors are already developing and deploying agentic SOC capabilities, including systems designed to investigate incidents across endpoint, identity, cloud, SaaS and network environments.
Will AI make cyberattacks faster?
AI can potentially reduce the time and expertise required for parts of offensive cyber activity. Security researchers and vendors are therefore increasingly focused on defending against AI-accelerated attacks.
Conclusion
AI agents are changing cybersecurity from a largely alert-driven discipline toward a more continuous, investigative and increasingly autonomous model.
They can potentially collect evidence, investigate incidents, analyse threats, monitor identities, assess vulnerabilities and execute approved responses.
Their greatest advantage may be speed.
Cyberattacks can evolve quickly, and human analysts cannot manually investigate every signal generated by modern digital environments.
Agentic cybersecurity offers a way to increase defensive capacity by allowing AI systems to handle more of the investigative workload.
But autonomy also creates a new security problem.
The defenders' AI must itself be secured.
Agents require identities, permissions, monitoring and governance. They must be protected against prompt injection, excessive privileges, compromised tools and incorrect actions.
The future is therefore unlikely to be:
Humans replaced by AI.
It is more likely to be:
Human security professionals + specialized AI agents + governed automation.
The organizations that get this balance right could gain a significant defensive advantage.
The goal is not to give AI unlimited control.
It is to make AI capable of seeing more, investigating faster and acting safely, while keeping human judgment at the points where it matters most.

ai_security.title: E2A-Bench: Benchmarking Evidence-to-Action Reliability in Financial Chart Reasoning
ai_security.abstract: Can financial vision-language models (VLMs) turn chart evidence into reliable action recommendations? Existing hallucination evaluations are mostly claim-centric; they assess whether generated statements are supported, but not whether evidence remains traceable through rationale, confidence, and final action. We introduce E2A-Bench, a 969-query benchmark for financial chart reasoning, constructed from 323 HS300 constituents under three input modalities with deterministic OHLCV-derived evidence anchors. E2A-Bench evaluates grounding, reasoning-action consistency, evidence-confidence calibration, and directional coverage through UCR, RCI, ECI, and NDR, where NDR measures coverage-aware evidence-to-action reliability rather than realized trading performance. Evaluating 20 VLMs reveals three failures hidden by scalar hallucination scores: the lowest-UCR model ranks near the bottom by NDR due to only 6.4% directional coverage; oracle-aided verification reduces unsupported claims but can collapse coverage; and financial fine-tuning amplifies the BUY:SELL ratio by factors of 4.21 to 4.68 across strict base-fine-tuned pairs. These results show that financial VLM evaluation should trace the full evidence-to-action chain rather than rely on a single hallucination score. Code and data: https://github.com/wanng-ide/E2A-Bench
